measures.questionText: A TRANSPARENT, ACCOUNTABLE, MODERN COUNTY GOVERNMENT Shall the San Diego County Charter be amended to establish an Independent Ethics Commission, Independent Budget Analyst, Independent Program Auditor, confirmation of certain senior County leaders, and optional Board of Supervisors appointment of the Public Defender; increase term limits from two to three terms for the Board of Supervisors members; require public disclosure of spending and performance data; clarify non-interference provisions; and update terminology and structure?
measures.officialStatement:
COUNTY COUNSEL IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS
BALLOT MEASURE TO AMEND COUNTY OF SAN DIEGO CHARTER
The Board of Supervisors (“Board”) for the County of San Diego
(“County”) placed this measure on the ballot. If approved by a majority of the
votes cast, this measure will amend the County Charter (“Charter”) as
specified in full text of the ballot measure.
The Charter provides for the structure of the County’s government,
including the powers and duties of its officers. The Charter can only be
amended with voter approval.
The following summarizes the amendments to the Charter proposed by
this measure:
• Increase County Supervisors’ term limits from two terms to three
terms. This amendment would allow a person to serve in the role of
County Supervisor for a maximum of twelve years, as opposed to
the current maximum of eight years. Any current or former
Supervisor’s prior time in office would count towards this three-term
limit.
• Require the Board to establish a procedure to review and confirm
Chief Administrative Officer appointment of the Assistant Chief
Administrative Officer, Deputy Chief Administrative Officers,
Director of the Office of Emergency Services, Public Health Officer,
and Public Defender. The Board shall have the power to remove
such officers, with or without cause, by 4/5ths vote.
• The Board may appoint an Independent Budget Analyst and
Independent Program Auditor. These new positions would perform
specified audit and budget services as directed by the Board or, for
the Independent Budget Analyst a County Supervisor. The Board
may appoint one person to serve in both positions.
• The Board may change Public Defender to a Board appointment
rather than Chief Administrative Officer appointment and may
appoint additional officers that do not duplicate the Chief
Administrative Officer’s functions.
• Provides examples of permissible practices that County Supervisors
may engage in without violating the non-interference clause.
• Update Charter to state that no County Officer may influence the
Director of Purchasing and Contracting for illegal personal gain or
as prohibited by Charter’s non-interference clause. Currently, the
Charter provides that no County Officer may influence Purchasing
Agent in performance of duty and that Board may only conduct
official business with Purchasing Agent at a regular Board meeting.
• Change Citizen Advisory Board to Community Advisory Board and
update appointment criteria.
• Direct Board to establish an Ethics Commission of seven
commissioners to be confirmed by the Board; one appointed by
each County Supervisor and two by County Counsel.
Commissioners are subject to removal, term limits, and certain
qualifications as specified in the full measure text and may be
granted subpoena power.
• Require the Auditor and Controller to post all County spending data
to the County’s website and order an annual independent financial
and performance audit of County expenditures, made available to
the public.
• Clarify that regulation of political activities does not prohibit activities
allowed by law.
• Update prohibition against nepotism by specifying degree of
relation.
• Updates Charter structure and terminology.
A “yes” vote is a vote in favor of the proposed Charter amendments.
A “no” vote is a vote against amending the Charter.

provenance.quote: A TRANSPARENT, ACCOUNTABLE, MODERN COUNTY GOVERNMENT Shall the San Diego County Charter be amended to establish an Independent Ethics Commission, Independent Budget Analyst, Independent Program Auditor, confirmation of certain senior County leaders, and optional Board of Supervisors appointment of the Public Defender; increase term limits from two to three terms for the Board of Supervisors members; require public disclosure of spending and performance data; clarify non-interference provisions; and update terminology and structure?

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Amend San Diego County’s charter to increase supervisors’ limit from two four-year terms to three, counting prior service under the partial-term rules below. Require a seven-member ethics commission and allow the board to appoint an independent budget analyst and program auditor, including one person serving both roles. Require board review and confirmation of specified senior appointments, with a separate option for the board to appoint the public defender. Require public online spending data and an annual independent financial and performance audit of county expenditures. The package also clarifies the non-interference and purchasing rules, updates community advisory-board appointments, political-activity and family-hiring provisions, and modernizes charter terminology. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the entire charter-amendment package, including the three-term supervisor limit and the oversight, appointment and disclosure changes.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the existing charter, including its two-term supervisor limit, rather than adopt this amendment package.

parts.label: Supervisor term counting
parts.what: The limit would be three terms regardless of which supervisor district a person represents. Current and former supervisors’ prior service counts. A person elected or appointed to an unexpired term who serves more than half a full four-year term is counted as serving a full term. A supervisor who resigns or is removed with less than half a term remaining is also counted as serving a full term. The rule therefore includes specific treatment of partial terms, rather than a simple promise of twelve years for every person.

parts.label: Ethics commission membership
parts.what: The board must establish the commission by ordinance. Each supervisor appoints one member and County Counsel appoints two; all require majority board confirmation. Members serve without pay in staggered four-year terms and must remain county residents and be current or former judges, attorneys, educators or professionals experienced in professional, government or corporate ethics and accountability, with no prohibited conflicts. After a full four-year term, a member must wait at least two years before reappointment. The charter also bars commissioners and commission staff from seeking elective office unless the election is at least two years after the commissioner’s last day of service. Vacancies must be filled within 90 days for the remaining term. Five of seven commissioners may remove a member for cause; the board also retains removal authority under the charter’s appointive-officer rule.

parts.label: Ethics investigations
parts.what: The commission investigates signed ethics complaints involving people in elective office, makes findings and recommendations using a clear-and-convincing-evidence standard, and publicly reports both substantiated and unsubstantiated findings. Additional related duties may be set by ordinance. Subpoena and oath powers are optional and require a board ordinance. Commission rules and appointment of necessary staff remain subject to board approval.

parts.label: Budget analyst and program auditor
parts.what: The board may appoint one or two people for these roles and may remove them by majority vote. The budget analyst responds to board direction or an individual supervisor’s request, analyzing revenues, costs, budget assumptions, policy options and long-term fiscal risks and publishing accessible findings. The analyst must have the specified professional or educational qualifications and municipal-finance or equivalent experience. The program auditor evaluates county programs and proposed initiatives, outcomes and cost-effectiveness, alternatives and corrective actions at board direction. The board sets the evaluation’s scope and design, while the auditor retains professional independence over analysis, conclusions and public reporting.

parts.label: Senior appointments and removal
parts.what: The board must create a process to review and confirm the chief administrative officer’s appointments of assistant and deputy chief administrative officers, the emergency-services director, public health officer and public defender when not appointed directly by the board. It may designate additional officers by ordinance. Except where the charter provides otherwise, these officers serve at the chief administrative officer’s pleasure and may also be removed by four-fifths of the board, with or without cause. The board may separately make the public defender a direct board appointment and create additional independent evaluative offices that do not duplicate the chief administrative officer’s functions.

parts.label: Supervisors, staff and purchasing
parts.what: The general prohibition on directing or interfering with staff appointed under the chief administrative officer remains. Clarifications allow lawful information requests; assistance with supervisor initiatives under board policy and prompt notice to the chief administrative officer; use of internal services under the usual rules; and input on hiring or dismissal of specified unclassified managers. Violations remain infractions, with supervisor violations also misconduct in office. The purchasing provision would prohibit influence or coercion for illegal personal gain or contrary to the non-interference rule, replacing the prior broader purchasing-agent wording.

parts.label: Spending disclosure and other changes
parts.what: The auditor and controller must post all county spending data online in an accessible format, order an annual independent accountant’s financial and performance audit, publish findings and implement oversight of corrective actions. Citizen advisory boards become community advisory boards, with appointments reflecting affected communities and their geographic, cultural, socioeconomic and other characteristics. The political-activity rule would expressly preserve activities by elected officials and their staff that state and federal law allow. The family-hiring ban specifies the fourth degree of relationship and retains its exception for people appointed before that provision’s operative date. Other changes update structure and terminology.
